summary: This informational RFC defines key management attributes used by the US National Security Agency. They can appear in asymmetric and symmetric key packages and in the CMS content types that wrap those packages, as in RFCs 5958 and 6031.

plainLanguage.summary: Labels the NSA attaches to cryptographic keys, saying how a key may be handled.

questions: what is nsa cms key management
how do you classify cryptographic keys
subtitle: Attributes for managing cryptographic keys in CMS packages

tldr.problem: Organizations like the NSA need to attach management information to cryptographic keys, such as their purpose, how they should be used, who may receive them, and their classification level, but no standard attributes existed for this in CMS.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7906 defines a comprehensive set of attributes that can be added to key packages, including key purpose, key use, validity periods, distribution restrictions, nomenclature, and classification labels.
tldr.outcome: System administrators can now consistently label and manage cryptographic keys using standardized attributes in CMS packages, improving interoperability and consistency across organizations.

today: RFC 7906 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the standard specification for NSA CMS key management attributes, used by organizations managing cryptographic keys in government and defense systems.

sections.title: Key Attributes and CMS
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is a standard way to wrap and protect cryptographic keys and other content. CMS supports a variety of content types such as SignedData, EnvelopedData, and key packages themselves. Each of these content types can carry attributes, which are pieces of metadata that describe or constrain the content.

Key management requires more than just the cryptographic material itself. Organizations need to track and enforce rules about when a key may be used, who may receive it, what purpose it serves, how long it remains valid, and other management constraints. This RFC defines a collection of attributes that serve these management functions, allowing system administrators to attach standardized metadata to keys without needing to design custom solutions.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ship a package, you attach a label with the address, weight, and handling instructions. Cryptographic keys are similar: you need labels saying who can have them, what they are for, and when they expire.

sections.title: Key Naming and Identification
sections.content:
The TSEC Nomenclature attribute provides the name for a piece of keying material. This includes a printable short title of up to 32 alphanumeric characters, plus optional edition, register, and segment identifiers for organizing and tracking multiple related keys. For example, an organization might deliver daily keys for a month in one package; the nomenclature identifies the month as the edition and the specific day as the segment.

The Key Algorithm attribute specifies the cryptographic algorithm and format of the key material, including optional check-word and Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) algorithms. The Key Package Receivers attribute indicates which organizations or devices are authorized to receive and use the key package, helping intermediaries make routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: TSEC names keys like a mail system: the month is the edition, the day is the segment, and the short title is the street address. The key algorithm says what type of lock the key works with.

sections.title: Key Purpose and Use
sections.content:
The Key Purpose attribute specifies the intended context for the key, with values including Operational (A), Training (T), Exercise (X), Testing (Z), Maintenance (M), and others. This allows organizations to separate keys used in real operations from those used for training or testing.

The Key Use attribute specifies the cryptographic function, with values such as Traffic Encryption Key (TEK), Key Encryption Key (KEK), Message Signature Key (MSK), and many others specific to NSA naming conventions. For example, a Key Production Key is used to seed a keystream generator for producing other keys, while a Transmission Security Key protects against interception without relying on cryptanalysis.

Together, these attributes allow fine-grained control over key deployment. A key marked as Training/TEK cannot be accidentally used for operational encryption, preventing accidental security violations.
sections.plainLanguage: Key purpose says whether the key is for real use, training, or testing. Key use says what the key does: is it for encrypting data, signing documents, or unlocking other keys? Together, they ensure the right key is used in the right place.

sections.title: Key Validity and Constraints
sections.content:
The Key Validity Period attribute specifies explicit start and end dates for when a key may be used, with fields doNotUseBefore and optionally doNotUseAfter. The Key Duration attribute specifies the maximum length of time a key may be used, measured in hours, days, weeks, months, or years, allowing maximum durations like 96 hours or 100 years.

The Key Distribution Period attribute specifies when the key package may be distributed to recipients. The Key Province attribute identifies the scope, range, or jurisdiction in which the key is to be used, indicating geographic or organizational boundaries.

These temporal and spatial constraints prevent keys from being used outside their intended operational window or boundary, improving the security of the overall key management infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: These attributes answer: When can you use this key? For how long? Where can you use it? A key might be good only from Monday to Friday, or only in one country, or only for the next 30 days.

sections.title: Classification and Access Control
sections.content:
The Classification attribute applies a security label to the key package, indicating the sensitivity of the keying material. The security label includes a security-policy-identifier (an object identifier specifying which policy applies), an optional security-classification (using the basic hierarchy of unmarked, unclassified, restricted, confidential, secret, and top-secret), and optional security-categories for finer granularity.

Security categories are divided into Enumerated Tags and Informative Tags. An Enumerated Tag lists specific non-negative integers representing security attributes such as compartments or release permissions. An Informative Tag provides additional information that does not control access but may be displayed to users.

The RFC specifies that implementations MUST NOT make access control decisions based on privacy-marks, but MUST reject key packages if they contain a security policy identifier the receiver does not recognize and the label includes security categories. This design ensures that unknown security policies are treated conservatively.
sections.plainLanguage: Classification says how secret the key is: unclassified, confidential, secret, or top-secret. Security categories are like access codes that say which teams or countries are allowed to use the key.

sections.title: Other Key Attributes
sections.content:
The Community Identifiers attribute lists the communities authorized to receive the signed content, using either community object identifiers or hardware module lists. The Manifest attribute lists the short titles of all TSEC Nomenclature attributes from inner key packages, providing a summary of what keying material is included.

The Binary Signing Time attribute records the time at which a signature or Message Authentication Code was applied. The User Certificate attribute specifies the type, format, and value of an X.509 certificate in asymmetric key packages. The Split Identifier attribute designates that the keying material contains only one half of a split key (split keys are split into A and B halves), indicating which half is present and optionally the algorithm to combine the halves.

The RFC also defines attributes for key transport, key wrapping algorithms, certificate pointers, and various other management functions, all organized to work consistently across multiple layers of CMS encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: There are many more attributes like a metadata toolkit: who approved the key, when it was signed, whether it is split in half with another copy elsewhere, what algorithm to use to encrypt it for storage, and where to find related certificates.
